description: We’re a team of six building practical ways to explore how Earth is changing, using NASA data to turn complex observations into something people can actually understand and use.
summary: GEONEXSER turns NISAR radar observations into evidence anyone can trace, challenge, and trust. It presents seven real studies — floods in two Bangladeshi haors and in Chókwè, Mozambique; forest change in Rondônia; ground movement at Hayli Gubbi and Kīlauea; and soil moisture in Naogaon — on one interactive platform where every number links back to its method, quality screen, and source granule. It helps disaster responders, researchers, and citizens see through cloud and darkness without taking any claim on faith: results without independent support are labelled inconclusive, in plain sight.
details:
The challenge: NISAR's radar sees the Earth's surface through cloud and darkness, but raw radar data is unreadable to the people who need it most — disaster responders, researchers, and local decision-makers. Worse, a radar signal can mean more than one thing, so a pretty map without provenance can mislead. GeoNexSAR answers the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge by making surface change visible, comparable over time, and — above all — checkable.

How it works: a documented processing pipeline turns NISAR observations into seven published studies across four domains. Wetland flood candidates come from NISAR L2 GCOV backscatter change (Tanguar Haor, Hakaluki Haor, Chókwè); forest change candidates from persistent GCOV change in Rondônia; ground movement from NISAR and Sentinel-1 interferograms (GUNW) at Hayli Gubbi and Kīlauea; soil-moisture series from NISAR L3 SME2 in Naogaon. Every publication is fingerprinted (SHA-256) and passes a quality screen before it appears. The platform then lets anyone explore: a 3D globe of all studies, a scenes browser covering 1,142 NISAR acquisitions for a single day, time machines that scrub each study date by date, a temporal studio lining every study up against time, a hypotheses lab that argues alternative explanations against the evidence, side-by-side comparison, and a lineage graph that walks any number back to its method, quality screen, acquisitions, and independent reference. The interface is keyboard-navigable with screen-reader labels, and the demo video carries captions.

Tools used: the platform is a web application built with Next.js and React (TypeScript), with Three.js powering the 3D globe, Leaflet for the maps, and Recharts for the charts. The detection and comparison pipeline is written in Python, and published study artifacts are checksummed (SHA-256) and verified in continuous integration (GitHub Actions with automated browser tests). No special hardware is needed — it runs in any modern browser.

What makes it different is honesty as a feature. No study here claims validation — the validation column is empty for all seven, by evidence, and the platform says so. Independent reference checks (optical imagery, flood maps) are reported as support, never proof; radar movement is labelled apparent line-of-sight, never vertical displacement; soil moisture is never presented as crop stress or drought. Empty and inconclusive states are shown, not hidden. The team weighed this throughout: a tool that overstates what radar can prove would do real harm to the responders relying on it, so every design choice favours showing uncertainty over looking certain.

What we'd build next: disproof conditions for every claim. Each study would state, in plain language, the exact observation that would overturn its conclusion — for Chókwè, one cloud-free optical pass over the area within days of 17 January showing dry ground — and the platform would watch for that observation and update the verdict when it arrives. Science advances by trying to prove itself wrong; we would build that into the interface, so every number carries not just its evidence, but the evidence that would defeat it. Alongside that: more dates and regions as NISAR coverage grows, and partnerships with field teams for ground validation.
